text: Picture ten product teams, each shipping a different service, each on its own Kubernetes namespace, its own Terraform modules, its own CI pipeline. Nobody decided this on purpose — it's what happens by default when every team is fully responsible for its own path to production. That default has a real cost, and this lesson is about naming it precisely, because the whole discipline of platform engineering only makes sense once you understand exactly what problem it exists to solve.

Team A spends three weeks getting its first service through security review because nobody told them how ingress and secrets work here. Team B's pipeline looks nothing like Team A's, because the engineer who wrote it left, and whoever inherited it rebuilt it their own way. Multiply that by ten teams and you don't get ten slightly different setups — you get ten snowflake systems, each expensive to secure, patch, and support, and none of them documented well enough for anyone outside the team that built it to safely touch.

Team Topologies gives this a precise name: cognitive load. A stream-aligned team has a limited amount of mental capacity, and every piece of infrastructure complexity it has to understand and operate itself — instead of consuming as a ready-made capability — eats into that capacity and competes directly with what's left over for the actual business problem the team exists to solve. A platform exists for exactly one reason: to absorb that complexity once, instead of twenty teams each carrying their own copy of it.

CNCF's working definition is deliberately narrower than people assume: platform engineering builds toolchains and workflows that enable self-service capabilities. The output — an Internal Developer Platform — consolidates provisioning, deployment, and operational tooling behind that self-service interface. Notice what's missing from that definition: it isn't a ticket queue, which just relocates the bottleneck to a human; it isn't a mandate imposed with no feedback path; and it isn't a one-time migration project with an end date.

An IDP is a product — ongoing, maintained, and judged by whether the teams using it are genuinely better off. That distinction, between shipping infrastructure and running a product that other engineers choose to use, is exactly where this chapter goes next: treating the platform as a product, and treating every developer who touches it as a real customer whose feedback actually changes the roadmap.
